screening.reason: Reports a diagnostic prediction (ASD vs. TC) analysis of ABIDE resting-state fMRI functional connectivity and graph-theory features using a random SVM cluster (Inclusion 2, 3).

evidence_spans.text: Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data of 46 TC and 61 ASD patients were obtained from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) database. evidence_spans.text: Only 84 of 107 subjects are utilized in experiments because the translation or rotation of 7 TC and 16 ASD patients has surpassed ±2 mm or ±2◦. Then the random SVM cluster was proposed to distinguish TC and ASD. The results show that this method has an excellent classiﬁcation performance based on all the features. Furthermore, the accuracy based on the optimal feature set could reach to 96.15%. Abnormal brain regions could also be found, such as inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) (orbital and opercula part), hippocampus, and precuneus. It is indicated that the method of random SVM cluster may apply to the auxiliary diagnosis of ASD. Keywords: random support vector machine cluster, neuroimaging, autism spectrum disorder, classiﬁcation, feature selection INTRODUCTION Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is mainly reﬂected in the communication and language barriers, diﬃculties in social communication, and it is a kind of neurological developmental disorder (Karten and Hirsch, 2015; Khundrakpam et al., 2017). The behavioral phenotype of ASD is well-depicted but its etiology and pathogenesis is rarely known (Amaral et al., 2008). According to the results of Hallmayer et al. (2011), the causes of ASD mainly include genetic and environmental risk factors. Some of the symptoms of ASD generally appear in about 2 years old (Ecker et al., 2015), thus the early diagnosis is needed (Plitt et al., 2015). It is recognized that traditional clinical methods cannot well distinguish patients from healthy controls (HC) (Mwangi et al., 2012). And it may not be complex enough to capture the abnormal brain regions in individuals who suﬀering from ASD (Uddin et al., 2011). To avoid this disadvantage, machine learning is introduced in the neuroimaging ﬁeld. It is a valid means to extract messages from neuroimaging data and further predict the future changes of the disease (Klöppel et al., 2012; Orrù et al., 2012). Among numerous machine learning methods, support vector machines (SVM) is an excellent classiﬁcation method Bi et al. Classiﬁcation of ASD Using Random-SVM-Cluster (Zhang et al., 2015). SVM has distinct merits such as the higher classiﬁcation accuracy (Zhang and Wu, 2012) and no need for a large number of training samples to avoid over-ﬁtting (Li et al., 2010). Thus, SVM has aroused widespread concern of researchers in the ﬁeld of neuroimaging (Sundermann et al., 2014). In the researches of machine learning, SVM has been applied to classify ASD from corresponding controls. Gori et al. (2015) extracted features from the gray matter subregions, then these features were used in SVM to identity ASD from HC and the area under ROC curve (AUC) is 0.74. Jin et al. (2015) proposed an original multi-kernel SVM classiﬁcation method to classify ASD from HC and the accuracy can reach to 76%. Chen et al. (2016) used the SVM to classify 112 adolescent subjects with ASD and 128 HC, and the classiﬁcation accuracy was 79.17%. Odriozola et al. (2015) used the SVM based on functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data to classify 20 children with ASD and 20 typically developing (TD) peers, and the result showed 85% classiﬁcation accuracy. Chanel et al. (2016) used the method of SVM and Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) based on fMRI data to classify ASD from HC, and the result showed good classiﬁcation accuracy (up to 92.3%). These SVM classiﬁcation studies on ASD have achieved relatively high classiﬁcation accuracy in the range of 70–93% compared with traditional methods. They usually employed a single SVM and common features such as functional connections, gray matter volume to classify ASD from HC, and the classiﬁcation accuracy is generally lower than 90%. In this paper, a novel method of random SVM cluster is proposed and several graph metrics of brain functional connectivity (e.g., local eﬃciency, shortest path) are employed to classify ASD and typical controls (TC). This method has some good performance. Firstly, the classiﬁcation accuracy reaches to a higher level based on all the features. Then, we could ﬁnd out the optimal feature set, the classiﬁcation accuracy could also reach to the same level based on the optimal feature set. Thirdly, on the basis of the optimal feature set, we could ﬁnd out the abnormal brain regions such as inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) (orbital and opercula part), hippocampus, and precuneus. Thus, the random SVM cluster may apply to the auxiliary diagnosis of ASD. MATERIALS AND METHODS Demographic Information The Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) database (http://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.org/indi/abide/) (Di Martino et al., 2014) contains a variety of neuroimaging data. And the resting-state fMRI data include 539 ASD and 573 age-matched TC. There are 12 kinds of image protocols. This study chooses one of the image protocols, details as follows. MRI scanner = 3.0- T Siemens, TR = 3,000 ms, TE = 28 ms, data matrix = 64∗64, Pixel Spacing X = 3.0 mm, Pixel Spacing Y = 3.0 mm, Flip Angle = 90◦, Slice Thickness = 0.0 mm, no slice gap, axial slices = 34, time points = 120. Finally, 61 subjects with ASD and 46 TC met the image protocol. The original studies included in ABIDE received approval from each site’s Institutional Review Board (IRB). All images were obtained with informed consent according to procedures established by human subject research boards. Only 84 of 107 subjects are utilized in experiments because the translation or the rotation of 7 TC and 16 ASD patients has surpassed ± 2 mm or ± 2◦.

evidence_spans.text: TABLE 1 | Basic information of ASD and TC. Variables (Mean ± SD) Autism (n = 45) TC (n = 39) P value Gender (M/F) 41/4 33/6 0.359 Age (years) 13.4 ± 2.4 12.9 ± 1.7 0.278 ASD, Autism spectrum disorder; TC, typical controls.
evidence_spans.claim: Final analysed sample: 45 ASD, 39 TC, matched on age and gender.

evidence_spans.text: all the fMRI images are preprocessed by the Data Processing Assistant for Resting- State fMRI (DPARSF) software (Cui et al., 2015) (http://d.rnet. co/DPABI/DPABI_V2.3_170105.zip). The whole preprocessing procedures include:(1) Converting DICOM to NIFTI, (2) Removing the ﬁrst 10 time points, (3) Slicing timing, (4) Realigning, (5) Normalizing with the echo-planar imaging (EPI) template, (6) Smoothing, (7) Removing the linear trend, (8) Temporal ﬁltering, (9) Removing covariates.
evidence_spans.claim: All fMRI images were preprocessed using DPARSF software.

evidence_spans.text: fMRI image could be divided into 90 regions based on the Automatic Anatomical Labeling (AAL) (Tzourio-Mazoyer et al., 2002) atlas. We make these regions as the nodes of brain network, so there are 90 nodes. An average of the time series of a region’s all voxels can be used to capture the mean time series of this region (Khazaee et al., 2016). The average time series of every two brain regions can be employed to calculate the Pearson correlation coeﬃcient which is made as the link of the brain network (Khazaee et al., 2015), so there are 4,005 (90∗89/2) weighted edges.
evidence_spans.claim: The brain was parcellated into 90 regions using the AAL atlas, yielding 4,005 pairwise connectivity edges.

evidence_spans.text: Firstly, the 84 samples are divided into 58 training samples and 26 test samples based on the ratio of 7:3. Then 50 samples are randomly selected from the 58 training samples and 62 features are randomly selected from 4,225 features, which form a single SVM using Radial Basis Function (RBF) as kernel provided by the SVM toolbox (http://see.xidian.edu.cn/faculty/chzheng/ bishe/indexﬁles/indexl.htm) (Gunn, 1998). The width argument of RBF equals to 3, and penalty coeﬃcient equals to Inf. The process is repeated for 500 times and these 500 SVMs constitute into a random SVM cluster.
evidence_spans.claim: The 84 samples were split once into 58 training and 26 test samples (ratio 7:3) to build and evaluate the random SVM cluster.

evidence_spans.text: the accuracy of the random SVM cluster is as high as 96.15%. This is suﬃcient to show that the performance of the random SVM cluster is much better than a single SVM.
evidence_spans.claim: The random SVM cluster achieved 96.15% accuracy, much higher than a single SVM.

A single 70/30 train/test split (58/26 subjects) is used, with no cross-validation or repeated splits reported, and the optimal number of base classifiers and the optimal feature-set dimensionality (q) are both selected by maximising accuracy on the same 26-subject test set that is then reported as the final result: "Firstly, the 84 samples are divided into 58 training samples and 26 test samples based on the ratio of 7:3. Then 50 samples are randomly selected from the 58 training samples and 62 features are randomly selected from 4,225 features, which form a single SVM using Radial Basis Function (RBF) as kernel provided by the SVM toolbox (http://see.xidian.edu.cn/faculty/chzheng/ bishe/indexﬁles/indexl.htm) (Gunn, 1998). The width argument of RBF equals to 3, and penalty coeﬃcient equals to Inf. The process is repeated for 500 times and these 500 SVMs constitute into a random SVM cluster."

risk_of_bias.summary: Cohort exclusion and the pipeline/atlas are clearly reported, but the headline 96.15% accuracy comes from a single train/test split in which both the optimal number of base classifiers and the optimal feature-set size were tuned by maximising accuracy on that same held-out test set, with no independent validation set or cross-validation — a clear instance of test-set leakage via hyperparameter and feature-set selection.

charting.feature_extraction_tools: DPARSF (Data Processing Assistant for Resting-State fMRI)
charting.specific_features: ROI-wise Pearson correlation functional connectivity (AAL atlas, 90 ROIs, 4,005 edges) plus graph-theory metrics (degree, shortest path, local efficiency, clustering coefficient) at a 0.25 connectivity threshold
charting.model_category: Ensemble of support vector machines (random SVM cluster)
charting.specific_algorithms: Random SVM cluster (500 bootstrap-sampled, feature-subsampled RBF-kernel SVMs with majority voting); compared against a single SVM
charting.validation_methodology: Single random 70/30 split (58 training / 26 test subjects); the optimal number of base classifiers and the optimal feature-set dimensionality were both chosen by maximising accuracy on the same 26-subject test set
charting.key_performance_results: The random SVM cluster reached 96.15% accuracy on the 26-subject test set using the optimal feature set (272 features), compared to lower accuracy for a single SVM.
charting.features_associated_disorder: Abnormal regions identified included inferior frontal gyrus (orbital and opercular parts), hippocampus, precuneus, and cingulate gyrus.
charting.dataset_openly_available: No statement of code or participant-list availability found in the text.

narrative_row.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction (ensemble SVM) using ABIDE I resting-state fMRI from subjects sharing one scan protocol, n=84 (45 ASD/39 TC) after excluding 23 subjects for excessive motion.
narrative_row.methods: DPARSF-preprocessed functional connectivity (AAL atlas, 90 ROIs, 4,005 edges) plus graph-theory metrics, classified with a random cluster of 500 bootstrap/feature-subsampled SVMs (majority vote), evaluated on a single 70/30 train/test split.
narrative_row.outcomes: The random SVM cluster achieved 96.15% test accuracy with an optimal 272-feature subset, far exceeding a single SVM; discriminative regions included inferior frontal gyrus, hippocampus, precuneus and cingulate gyrus.
narrative_row.key_limitations: Headline accuracy is derived from a single train/test split in which both the ensemble size and the feature-set dimensionality were tuned by maximising accuracy on that same test set, with no cross-validation or independent validation set; diagnostic label source not described; no code/participant-list availability statement; small, single-protocol sample.
narrative_row.relevance_notes: A cautionary example for the review: the very high reported accuracy (96.15%) on a small single-protocol ABIDE subset is attributable to test-set leakage during hyperparameter/feature-set selection rather than independently validated generalisation performance.

kg_link.cohort_description: Subjects selected from ABIDE I by matching a single MRI acquisition protocol (3.0T Siemens, TR=3000ms, TE=28ms); after excluding 7 TC and 16 ASD for motion >2mm translation or >2deg rotation, 45 ASD and 39 TC (n=84) were analysed.
kg_link.sites: not named (subjects selected by matching one specific scan protocol across the ABIDE database, not by named site)
kg_link.pipeline: DPARSF (Data Processing Assistant for Resting-State fMRI)
kg_link.finding: A random SVM cluster achieved 96.15% accuracy on a single 26-subject test split using an optimal 272-feature set, substantially outperforming a single SVM; however, both the ensemble size and feature-set size were tuned on that same test set, indicating test-set leakage.
evidence_quotes: Only 84 of 107 subjects are utilized in experiments because the translation or rotation of 7 TC and 16 ASD patients has surpassed ±2 mm or ±2◦. Then the random SVM cluster was proposed to distinguish TC and ASD. The results show that this method has an excellent classiﬁcation performance based on all the features. Furthermore, the accuracy based on the optimal feature set could reach to 96.15%. Abnormal brain regions could also be found, such as inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) (orbital and opercula part), hippocampus, and precuneus. It is indicated that the method of random SVM cluster may apply to the auxiliary diagnosis of ASD. Keywords: random support vector machine cluster, neuroimaging, autism spectrum disorder, classiﬁcation, feature selection INTRODUCTION Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is mainly reﬂected in the communication and language barriers, diﬃculties in social communication, and it is a kind of neurological developmental disorder (Karten and Hirsch, 2015; Khundrakpam et al., 2017). The behavioral phenotype of ASD is well-depicted but its etiology and pathogenesis is rarely known (Amaral et al., 2008). According to the results of Hallmayer et al. (2011), the causes of ASD mainly include genetic and environmental risk factors. Some of the symptoms of ASD generally appear in about 2 years old (Ecker et al., 2015), thus the early diagnosis is needed (Plitt et al., 2015). It is recognized that traditional clinical methods cannot well distinguish patients from healthy controls (HC) (Mwangi et al., 2012). And it may not be complex enough to capture the abnormal brain regions in individuals who suﬀering from ASD (Uddin et al., 2011). To avoid this disadvantage, machine learning is introduced in the neuroimaging ﬁeld. It is a valid means to extract messages from neuroimaging data and further predict the future changes of the disease (Klöppel et al., 2012; Orrù et al., 2012). Among numerous machine learning methods, support vector machines (SVM) is an excellent classiﬁcation method Bi et al. Classiﬁcation of ASD Using Random-SVM-Cluster (Zhang et al., 2015). SVM has distinct merits such as the higher classiﬁcation accuracy (Zhang and Wu, 2012) and no need for a large number of training samples to avoid over-ﬁtting (Li et al., 2010). Thus, SVM has aroused widespread concern of researchers in the ﬁeld of neuroimaging (Sundermann et al., 2014). In the researches of machine learning, SVM has been applied to classify ASD from corresponding controls. Gori et al. (2015) extracted features from the gray matter subregions, then these features were used in SVM to identity ASD from HC and the area under ROC curve (AUC) is 0.74. Jin et al. (2015) proposed an original multi-kernel SVM classiﬁcation method to classify ASD from HC and the accuracy can reach to 76%. Chen et al. (2016) used the SVM to classify 112 adolescent subjects with ASD and 128 HC, and the classiﬁcation accuracy was 79.17%. Odriozola et al. (2015) used the SVM based on functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data to classify 20 children with ASD and 20 typically developing (TD) peers, and the result showed 85% classiﬁcation accuracy. Chanel et al. (2016) used the method of SVM and Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) based on fMRI data to classify ASD from HC, and the result showed good classiﬁcation accuracy (up to 92.3%). These SVM classiﬁcation studies on ASD have achieved relatively high classiﬁcation accuracy in the range of 70–93% compared with traditional methods. They usually employed a single SVM and common features such as functional connections, gray matter volume to classify ASD from HC, and the classiﬁcation accuracy is generally lower than 90%. In this paper, a novel method of random SVM cluster is proposed and several graph metrics of brain functional connectivity (e.g., local eﬃciency, shortest path) are employed to classify ASD and typical controls (TC). This method has some good performance. Firstly, the classiﬁcation accuracy reaches to a higher level based on all the features. Then, we could ﬁnd out the optimal feature set, the classiﬁcation accuracy could also reach to the same level based on the optimal feature set. Thirdly, on the basis of the optimal feature set, we could ﬁnd out the abnormal brain regions such as inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) (orbital and opercula part), hippocampus, and precuneus. Thus, the random SVM cluster may apply to the auxiliary diagnosis of ASD. MATERIALS AND METHODS Demographic Information The Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) database (http://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.org/indi/abide/) (Di Martino et al., 2014) contains a variety of neuroimaging data. And the resting-state fMRI data include 539 ASD and 573 age-matched TC. There are 12 kinds of image protocols. This study chooses one of the image protocols, details as follows. MRI scanner = 3.0- T Siemens, TR = 3,000 ms, TE = 28 ms, data matrix = 64∗64, Pixel Spacing X = 3.0 mm, Pixel Spacing Y = 3.0 mm, Flip Angle = 90◦, Slice Thickness = 0.0 mm, no slice gap, axial slices = 34, time points = 120. Finally, 61 subjects with ASD and 46 TC met the image protocol. The original studies included in ABIDE received approval from each site’s Institutional Review Board (IRB). All images were obtained with informed consent according to procedures established by human subject research boards. Only 84 of 107 subjects are utilized in experiments because the translation or the rotation of 7 TC and 16 ASD patients has surpassed ± 2 mm or ± 2◦.
